session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: I will frame participants as men living everyday lives across different parts of the UK — not as research subjects or as representatives of 'masculinity'. The collective context is simply: men making food decisions, spending time with friends, living in specific places. The framing stays grounded in ordinary, concrete experience rather than identity categories, to reduce social desirability pressure from the outset.
priority_research_areas: Gender as an influence on food choice (Section 3): Participants are likely to initially deny that gender shapes their eating — 'I just eat what I like' is a predictable first move. Behavioural grounding and specific-moment probes will be essential to get past performance of indifference and into actual practice.

Social dynamics around plant-based eating (Sections 4–5): The group may quickly converge on a shared scepticism toward plant-based food. Consensus risk is highest here. I need to watch for social convergence masking real differentiation in openness or curiosity.

The role of other people in food decisions (Sections 2–3): Men in group contexts often understate the degree to which social norms shape their choices. I need to probe the gap between stated autonomy and described social behaviour — e.g. what happens when eating out with mates, at work, in front of a partner.

What 'would need to change' for plant-based eating (Section 4): Abstract answers ('I'd need to enjoy it more', 'it'd have to taste the same') are predictable. The research value is in specifics: which social situations are the hardest, what the practical blockers are, who in their lives would notice or react.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability: All participants are meat eaters in a study touching on plant-based eating. There is a risk they perform collective scepticism toward plant-based food — not because it reflects their actual views, but because it feels like the socially safe position in an all-male group. Use behavioural grounding early and consistently.

Consensus hardening on gender denial: The group is likely to quickly agree that 'gender doesn't really influence what I eat.' This may be partly true and partly a face-saving move. Plan a sharpening probe (e.g. a specific social scenario) before moving on from Section 3.

Group identity performance: In an all-male group discussing food and masculinity, there is a risk of competitive performance of meat-eating identity or indifference to health. Watch for this and probe the gap between public-facing answer and private behaviour.

Bilal's dietary context: Halal requirements are a real and practical dimension of food choice that may intersect with, but is not reducible to, the plant-based discussion. Don't conflate. If it surfaces, treat it as its own thread.

Tangent risk in Section 1 (male friendship): This warm-up section could run long if participants enjoy reminiscing. Keep it light but purposeful — the goal is to get a sense of social context, not a full social geography of each city.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: Hold back. Light touch throughout. Let participants establish their own register and comfort level. Avoid any probing that feels intrusive before rapport is built. Section 2: Moderate directivity — use behavioural grounding to get past generic answers ('I just eat what I fancy') toward specific contexts and decision moments. Sections 3–5 (main topics): Push harder. This is where the research value lives. Be willing to name tensions, invite dissent, surface contradictions, and hold the group on specifics rather than allowing abstract positions to stand unchallenged. Section 6: Light again. Give space for any final thoughts, but don't reopen closed threads or push for new depth when the session is winding down.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Sections 3, 4, and 5 are the three main_topic sections and together should receive the bulk of the word budget — roughly 55–60% of total. Sections 1 and 2 are context sections and get a moderate share — enough to build rapport and get usable grounding material, but not so much that they crowd the main topics. Sections 0 and 6 (intro and closing) are given a light budget — the opening only needs to welcome and instruct, and the close is a brief wind-down.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was purely introductory — participants introduced themselves by name, location, and age, with no substantive thematic content yet emerging. All five participants are men in their early-to-mid thirties from varied UK regions (Birmingham, Belfast, Bristol, London, Leeds). Occupational identities were consistently downplayed or described vaguely. The section closed with the moderator posing the first substantive question about favourite places to spend time with male friends.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator's approach here was standard warm-up framing: establishing psychological safety, clarifying format, and inviting brief self-introductions before moving to content. Participants engaged readily and without prompting, which suggests the opening tone landed well. No deeper facilitation was required or attempted at this stage — the priority was simply getting everyone comfortable and on the record before transitioning to the first real question.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on physical venues as social infrastructure, with participants converging on a pub/restaurant distinction that mapped onto different relational registers: the pub as low-effort, habitual, and ambient; sit-down meals (curry nights in particular) as more intentional and conducive to deeper conversation. A secondary thread emerged around low-commitment casual eating as a third category. Geographic variation was largely superficial — the underlying logic held consistently across all five cities.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section ran itself initially, with Henry and Bilal establishing a productive dynamic that others could step into. The main intervention was drawing in Sam and Connor individually, as both had stayed silent while the pattern solidified — a sensible move given the risk of two voices dominating early. Both added modest texture rather than genuinely new threads, which suggests the section had reached natural saturation. The transition away felt timely.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the phenomenology of habit: participants collectively worked through a distinction between automatic and deliberated choice, landing on the idea that meat-eating feels like a non-decision precisely because its underlying reasons — saturation, familiarity, culinary competence, social normalisation — are so thoroughly embedded they no longer surface. The framing of choice as 'invisible' rather than absent was the section's key conceptual yield, arrived at collaboratively rather than introduced by the moderator.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section was largely self-running between Noah and Sam, who built productively on each other without needing direction. The one intervention — drawing Connor in directly on the 'invisible choice' framing — worked efficiently: he confirmed and added the 'embedded reasons' gloss without derailing the thread. The transition question pivoting to gender was well-timed, catching the group at conceptual saturation and reorienting toward the next substantive territory without losing momentum.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section interrogated whether gender shapes food behaviour, landing on a distinction between performative and embedded masculinity — participants broadly rejected the former while acknowledging the latter. The more generative tension was between Bilal and Connor over whether 'automatic' and 'natural' are the same thing: Bilal resisted collapsing familiarity into naturalness; Connor argued that lived experience makes the distinction moot. Henry's 'package you get handed' framing usefully crystallised the section's conceptual endpoint.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section ran productively between Bilal and Connor without intervention until Henry was drawn in directly — a sensible move given the risk of a two-person loop excluding others. The decision to let the automatic/natural tension develop before intervening was well-judged; it reached genuine conceptual yield. Picking up Henry's 'package you get handed' phrase as a pivot into the hypothetical plant-based question was efficient, using participant language to mark closure before reorienting the group.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section examined the relationship between motivation and structural barriers to dietary change, landing on a productive distinction: friction and disinterest are not alternatives but co-constitutive — low motivation makes barriers feel larger, while real barriers persist regardless of motivation. The cooking knowledge gap, social visibility, and embedded dairy habits were named as concrete friction points. The section's conceptual yield was that neither 'I just don't want to' nor 'it's too difficult' fully explains inertia alone.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main move was opening Sam's layered account to the group immediately, which prompted Henry to challenge it productively — the Sam/Henry exchange then ran itself to genuine conceptual resolution without further intervention. Drawing Noah, Bilal, and Connor in at the close was necessary given their silence throughout; reframing toward 'what would make you genuinely want it' was a deliberate pivot away from barrier-cataloguing toward more generative territory for the next section.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on whether social normalisation and genuine wanting are the same thing or distinct. Noah and Bilal argued that normalisation generates wanting by reshaping what feels possible; Sam and Connor held that normalisation merely removes friction for a wanting that either pre-exists or doesn't — and for them, it largely doesn't. The section's conceptual yield was a clean distinction: normalisation is a necessary but insufficient condition for behavioural shift.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main move was sharpening a latent tension between Noah/Bilal and Sam into an explicit question — does normalisation create wanting or just remove a barrier? — then using Connor's London context as empirical ballast. Drawing Connor in directly was well-timed and produced the section's clearest formulation. Letting the Sam/Bilal exchange develop before intervening was the right call; the tension reached genuine resolution rather than being collapsed prematurely.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section refined the normalisation debate toward a deeper question: whether adult preferences are fixed or malleable. Noah argued that preferences are socially constructed from the outset, making them in principle re-shapeable; Connor conceded the construction point but held that early-built preferences resist later social change. The section's conceptual yield was a temporal distinction — origin and current fixity are separate questions — which left the group productively unresolved rather than converging.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main move was naming the unresolved tension explicitly in the closing framing — 'preference discovered versus developed' — rather than papering over it, which licensed Noah and Connor to keep refining rather than closing down. Repeated open invitations to Sam, Henry, and Bilal went unanswered, which is worth noting: the section ended as a two-voice exchange. Given it was the session close, that was acceptable, but earlier intervention might have broadened participation.
